domain_restrictions: f is a total function from the Euclidean plane R^2 to the two-element set {red,green}
A,B,C,P,O are points of the Euclidean plane R^2
the hypothesis applies only to triples A,B,C that are noncollinear (hence distinct) so the circumcenter is uniquely defined in R^2
the circumcenter operation circ(A,B,C) is the unique intersection of perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC (uses Euclidean geometry)
root_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every function f: R^2 -> {red,green}, if for all points A,B,C in R^2 that are noncollinear and satisfy f(A)=f(B)=f(C) we have f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A), then there exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c. Equivalently: ∀f [(∀A,B,C (noncollinear ∧ f(A)=f(B)=f(C) ⇒ f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A))) ⇒ (∃c ∈ {red,green} ∀P f(P)=c)].
quantifier_order: forall f : R^2 -> {red,green} (consider any 2-coloring of the plane)
assume (hypothesis) forall A,B,C in R^2: if A,B,C are noncollinear and f(A)=f(B)=f(C) then f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A)
conclude: exists c in {red,green} such that forall P in R^2, f(P) = c

payload.theorem_nl: Suppose that each point in the plane is colored either red or green, subject to the following condition: For every three noncollinear points $A,B,C$ of the same color, the center of the circle passing through $A,B$ and $C$ is also this color. Prove that all points of the plane are the same color.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Proceed by contradiction. Assume both colors occur, and choose O red and G green. Let R=dist(O,G). Use the geometric existence lemma to place five points X_1,...,X_5 on the circle centered at G with radius R, each equipped with a pair of support points A_i,B_i on the circle centered at O with radius R, with all ten support points distinct. Because O is red, the circle centered at O with radius R contains at most two green points. Hence among the five support pairs, at least three pairs are entirely red. For each such pair, the corresponding point X_i is the circumcenter of triangle O A_i B_i, so the circumcenter condition forces X_i to be red as well. Thus there are three distinct red points on the circle centered at G with radius R. Applying the circumcenter condition again to those three points shows that their circumcenter G is red, contradicting that G was chosen green. Therefore both colors cannot occur, so one color fills the whole plane.

steps.derives: Assume for contradiction that not all points of the plane have the same color. Since the codomain of f is exactly {red,green}, there exist points O,G in R^2 with f(O)=red and f(G)=green.
steps.trivial_justification: If the coloring is not constant, there exist two points of different colors. Because the only available colors are red and green, after renaming the two colors if necessary, one may choose O with f(O)=red and G with f(G)=green.

steps.derives: Let R = dist(O,G). Since O != G, we have R>0. By L3, choose five pairwise distinct points X_1,...,X_5 on the circle centered at G with radius R, and for each i choose points A_i,B_i so that A_i and B_i are exactly the two distinct intersections of the circle centered at O with radius R and the circle centered at X_i with radius dist(O,X_i); moreover the ten points A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5 are pairwise distinct.
steps.trivial_justification: The hypotheses of L3 hold because A1 gives O != G. The lemma supplies all auxiliary points and the pairwise-distinctness data needed later.

steps.derives: Among the ten pairwise distinct points A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5, at most two are green.
steps.trivial_justification: Each support point A_i or B_i lies on the circle centered at O with radius R by A2. Since f(O)=red by A1, L1 applied to the center O and radius R shows that on this circle there are at most two green points.

steps.derives: There exist three distinct indices i,j,k in {1,2,3,4,5} such that both points in each corresponding pair are red: f(A_i)=f(B_i)=red, f(A_j)=f(B_j)=red, and f(A_k)=f(B_k)=red.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L4 to the five pairs (A_1,B_1),...,(A_5,B_5). The premise 'at most two green among the ten points' is exactly A3, and the points are pairwise distinct by A2.

steps.derives: The three auxiliary points X_i,X_j,X_k are all red.
steps.trivial_justification: Consider index i. By A2, A_i and B_i are the two distinct intersections of circle(O,R) and circle(X_i,dist(O,X_i)). By A1 and A4, f(O)=f(A_i)=f(B_i)=red. Applying L2 gives f(X_i)=red. The same argument with j and k yields f(X_j)=red and f(X_k)=red.

By A2, the points X_i,X_j,X_k are distinct points on the circle centered at G with radius R. By A5 they all have the same color red. Therefore L5 applied to center G, radius R, and points X_i,X_j,X_k yields f(G)=red.

steps.derives: Contradiction. Therefore the assumption that the coloring is not constant is false.
steps.trivial_justification: A1 states f(G)=green, while A6 states f(G)=red.

steps.derives: There exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: Negating the conclusion means the coloring is nonconstant. Step A7 rules that out, so the coloring must be constant. Let c be the common value of f on the plane.

shared_context.content: A function f : R^2 -> {red, green} satisfies the circumcenter condition if for every noncollinear triple of points A,B,C in R^2, whenever f(A)=f(B)=f(C), the circumcenter of triangle ABC has the same color as A,B,C.
shared_context.label: Root hypothesis on the coloring

shared_context.content: For a point O in R^2 and real number r>0, the circle centered at O with radius r is {X in R^2 | dist(O,X)=r}. If three distinct points lie on one circle with center O, then O is the circumcenter of those three points. Any three distinct points on a circle are noncollinear, because a line meets a nondegenerate circle in at most two points.
shared_context.label: Circle and circumcenter conventions

candidates.strategy_summary: Use a contradiction built from two opposite-colored points O and G, a finite family of auxiliary circles, and a local color-transfer lemma. This differs from the failed attempts by avoiding any false global classification of circumcenter-closed subsets; the key steps explicitly use the 2-coloring and chosen points O,G. It also fixes the prior interface issue by stating the transfer lemma directly in terms of two explicit intersection points, so no extra radius hypothesis is missing, and it keeps the pairwise-distinct support-point information needed for the pigeonhole step.
